title: Beyond engagement: demographic, temporal, and topic variation in misinformation exposure on Facebook across European media systemic regions
screen_reason: Behavioural trace study of Facebook VIEWS (Meta/Social Science One URL Shares dataset, Jan 2017 - Nov 2022, EU27 + UK). Misinformation is operationalised as URLs fact-checked and labelled False by Meta-affiliated IFCN fact-checkers. The paper reports aggregated misinformation views per capita per month (Figure 5) and states one numeric point verbatim in the text: the March 2020 peak of ~0.2 views per capita, which the authors read as up to 20% of the European population seeing at least one misinformation story that month. That is a quantified exposure estimate with a denominator (population), so the paper is eligible. Almost all other results are demographic profiles (median age, % male) or topic descriptions, which are not prevalence shares.

estimates.country: EU 27 member states and the UK
estimates.date: January 2017 - November 2022; the extracted point is the peak month, March 2020
estimates.measure_type: Views of fact-checked-false URLs per capita per month on Facebook across the EU27+UK, at the series' peak month (March 2020)
estimates.value_raw: peak 'close to .2' misinformation views per capita in March 2020; authors read this as 'indicating that 20% of the European population saw at least one misinformation story in that month, assuming that each user viewed only one misinformation story'
estimates.denominator: Population of the EU27 + UK (views per capita); population size not stated numerically in the text
estimates.definition: A view is counted when a post containing the URL has been on a user's screen for more than 250 milliseconds; each action is logged once per user per URL. Numerator = views of URLs labelled False by Meta's IFCN fact-checking partners.
estimates.misinfo_def: “an umbrella term that includes all false or inaccurate information … groups together rumors, fake news, disinformation, propaganda, lies, and more”; operationalised as “content that has been fact-checked and labeled as false by an International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) fact-checker affiliated with Meta”
estimates.n: EU27+UK population (per-capita denominator; size not reported). Numerator drawn from 9,298 fact-checked-false URLs with 270,828 analysable rows.
estimates.source_quote: Note: For March 2020 there is a large spike in misinformation across Europe as is evident from the peak on the solid black line. ... The peak is close to .2 on the y-axis, indicating that 20% of the European population saw at least one misinformation story in that month, assuming that each user viewed only one misinformation story.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: URLs rated False by International Fact-Checking Network fact-checkers partnered with Meta's third-party fact-checking programme (operating in all 28 countries except Malta). No inter-rater reliability; authors note the operationalisation mirrors fact-checkers' coverage priorities and is conservative, while Allen et al. (2021) found the dataset may OVERestimate fake news by up to four times.
estimates.moderator_quote: The URL Shares dataset contains data from 46 countries in the period from January 2017 until November 2022. It contains 68,660,479 URLs ... The dataset contains URLs that have been (re-)shared over 100 times publicly on Facebook ... We filter this sample to 20,744 URLs that were labeled as False by Facebook's IFCN fact-checking partners.
estimates.notes: Read with care. (1) The value is an INTENSITY (views per capita per month), not a share of a news diet; the 20% figure is the authors' upper-bound reading of it and holds only under their stated assumption that no user saw more than one misinformation story. (2) The number is read off a figure ('close to .2'); no table of monthly values appears in the text. (3) It is a PEAK, not a representative month - the only monthly value stated numerically anywhere in the text, chosen because the instruction to collapse a time series to one point leaves no alternative. (4) All interaction counts carry differential-privacy noise; the authors filter to 'active months' (alpha = 0.0005) to keep the signal above it. (5) Sampling frame coded full_census because the underlying dataset is a platform-wide log of every URL publicly re-shared >100 times, but the misinformation numerator is limited to what fact-checkers happened to check, and the 100-reshare threshold excludes niche content, small countries and small languages. (6) Topic coded general_news because the corpus is cross-topic across 2017-2022, even though the top-10 stories in the extracted peak month were Covid-19 related.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) Figure 2(B), 'Percentage of total URLs top-shared within each country that was fact-checked as False', is a genuine CONTENT share by country - but no numeric value appears anywhere in the text, only the plotted figure and a ranking (Croatia, Greece, Lithuania, France, Slovakia highest per capita). Nothing extractable without the figure data or Supplementary Material 7. (b) The URL counts (20,744 URLs labelled False; 6,663 top-shared in EU/UK, 14,081 in the US; 9,298 after active-month filtering; a 28,000-URL non-misinformation control sample) cannot be turned into a content share: the 68,660,479-URL dataset total is for 46 countries and is NOT the denominator of the 20,744 (which comes from a country-filtered subsample), so any ratio would be a cross-denominator computation, barred by R8. The 28,000 control URLs are a deliberately sampled comparison set, not the population of non-misinformation URLs. (c) Table 1 and Table 2 (median age 41 and 47.2% male views for misinformation vs 40 / 40.1% for the control; by-region breakdowns) are demographic COMPOSITIONS of misinformation exposure, not shares of content or of exposure that is misinformation - no prevalence row. (d) 'women aged 35-44 were most exposed' and all topic-overlap counts (163 of top 200 URLs shared between genders, etc.) are comparative/descriptive, not prevalence shares. (e) No sharing prevalence: Figure 4 reports only the demographic profile of sharers, not a share of shares that were misinformation.

rob.design: Platform trace data (Meta/Social Science One URL Shares dataset), Jan 2017-Nov 2022, EU27+UK; inclusion requires a URL to have been publicly re-shared >100 times, which excludes niche content and small languages. Misinformation defined by Meta-partnered IFCN fact-checker 'False' labels (no researcher coding, no reliability statistic). Exposure = 'views' (>250 ms on screen, one per user per URL). All cells carry normally distributed differential-privacy noise; authors filter to 'active months' identified via a three-sigma empirical rule (alpha = 0.0005), retaining 6,002/6,663 (90%) EU/UK and 3,296/14,081 (23%) US-top-shared misinformation URLs. Known dataset bias: Allen et al. (2021) report the dataset may overestimate fake news by up to four times. Per-capita interpretation assumes uniform interactions within age groups.
